Permanental Inequalities and Unit Interval Orders

Sihong Pan   Mark Skandera   Jiayuan Wang Email: sip318@lehigh.edu  mas906@lehigh.edu  jiw922@lehigh.edu Affiliation: Lehigh University, Bethlehem PA, USA
Abstract

Given an n×nn\times n matrix A=(ai,j)A=(a_{i,j}) and I,J⊆[1,n]:={1,…,n}I,J\subseteq[1,n]:=\{1,\dotsc,n\}, let AI,J=(ai,j)i∈I,j∈JA_{I,J}=(a_{i,j})_{i\in I,j\in J} denote the (I,J)(I,J)-submatrix of AA. We consider a class of 00-11 totally nonnegative (TNN) matrices arising as antiadjacency matrices of unit interval orders, and show that for each matrix AA in this class, the inequalities

per⁡(A[1,h],[1,h])​per⁡(A[h+1,n],[h+1,n])≥per⁡(A[1,n]∩2​ℤ,[1,n]∩2​ℤ)​per⁡(A[1,n]∖2​ℤ,[1,n]∖2​ℤ)\perm(A_{[1,h],[1,h]})\perm(A_{[h+1,n],[h+1,n]})\;\geq\;\perm(A_{[1,n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z},[1,n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z}})\perm(A_{[1,n]\smallsetminus 2\mathbb{Z},[1,n]\smallsetminus 2\mathbb{Z}}) (∗*)

hold for h=1,…,n−1h=1,\dotsc,n-1.

Let 𝔄n\mathfrak{A}_{n} be the Young Subgroup 𝔖1,…,⌊n2⌋×𝔖⌈n2⌉,…,n\mathfrak{S}_{1,\dotsc,\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor}\times\mathfrak{S}_{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil,\dotsc,n}, and 𝔅n\mathfrak{B}_{n} be the parity alternating permutations {w=w1⋯wn∈𝔖n|i and wi have the same parity}\{w=w_{1}\cdots w_{n}\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\ |\ \text{$i$ and $w_{i}$ have the same parity}\}. We find a bijective map fn:𝔄n→𝔅nf_{n}:\mathfrak{A}_{n}\rightarrow\mathfrak{B}_{n} such that w≤fn​(w)w\leq f_{n}(w) under the Bruhat order for n≤13n\leq 13 and conjecture this holds for all nn. The existence of the bijective map fnf_{n} ensures that inequalities ( ∗ ) are satisfied for all TNN matrices AA when h=⌊n2⌋h=\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor. We also conjecture the inequalities ( ∗ ) to hold for all TNN matrices and all h=1,…,n−1h=1,\dotsc,n-1.

1 Introduction

Given an n×nn\times n matrix A=(ai,j)A=(a_{i,j}) and subsets I,J⊆[n]:={1,…,n}I,J\subseteq[n]:=\{1,\dotsc,n\}, define the submatrix AI,J=(ai,j)i∈I,j∈JA_{I,J}=(a_{i,j})_{i\in I,j\in J} of AA, and call det(AI,J)\det(A_{I,J}) a minor of AA. We call A∈Matn×n​(ℝ)A\in\mathrm{Mat}_{n\times n}(\mathbb{R}) totally nonnegative if each of its minors is negative. It is known that the defining inequalities det(AI,J)≥0\det(A_{I,J})\geq 0 of totally nonnegative matrices imply many other polynomial inequalities in the matrix entries. Some of these involve immanants of AA and its submatrices, i.e., linear combinations of the n!n! monomials {a1,w1⋯an,wn|w∈𝔖n}\{a_{1,w_{1}}\negthinspace\cdots a_{n,w_{n}}\,|\,w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\}. In particular for any function f:𝔖n→ℝf:\mathfrak{S}_{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, we define the ff-immanant of AA [13] to be the polynomial

Immf(A):=∑w∈𝔖nf(w)a1,w1⋯an,wn\mathrm{Imm}_{f}(A):=\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}f(w)a_{1,w_{1}}\negthinspace\cdots a_{n,w_{n}} (1.1)

generalizing the permanent and determinant

per(A)=∑w∈𝔖na1,w1⋯an,wn,det(A)=∑w∈𝔖nsgn(w)a1,w1⋯an,wn.\perm(A)=\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}a_{1,w_{1}}\negthinspace\cdots a_{n,w_{n}},\qquad\det(A)=\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\mathrm{sgn}(w)a_{1,w_{1}}\negthinspace\cdots a_{n,w_{n}}.

Skandera [10] gave a necessary and sufficient condition on subsets I,I′,J,J′⊆[n]:={1,…,n}I,I^{\prime},J,J^{\prime}\subseteq[n]:=\{1,\dotsc,n\} such that the inequality

det(AI,J)​det(A[n]∖I,[n]∖J)≤det(AI′,J′)​det(A[n]∖I′,[n]∖J′)\det(A_{I,J})\det(A_{[n]\smallsetminus I,[n]\smallsetminus J})\;\leq\;\det(A_{I^{\prime},J^{\prime}})\det(A_{[n]\smallsetminus I^{\prime},[n]\smallsetminus J^{\prime}})

holds whenever AA is TNN. Some other inequalities [2, 9, 14, 15] suggest that one can use inequalities involving determinants to produce inequalities involving permanents by simply changing the direction of the inequality.

Given a subset I⊆[n]I\subseteq[n], let I¯=[n]∖I\bar{I}=[n]\smallsetminus I. A natural starting point for such an investigation is Skandera’s result [10, Thm. 3.2] which provides an upper bound for all products det(AI,I)​det(AI¯,I¯)\det(A_{I,I})\det(A_{\bar{I},\bar{I}}):

det(AI,I)​det(AI¯,I¯)≤det(A[n]∩2​ℤ,[n]∩2​ℤ)​det(A[n]∖2​ℤ,[n]∖2​ℤ)\det(A_{I,I})\det(A_{\bar{I},\bar{I}})\;\leq\;\det(A_{[n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z},[n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z}})\det(A_{[n]\smallsetminus 2\mathbb{Z},[n]\smallsetminus 2\mathbb{Z}})

whenever AA is TNN. It is natural to ask whether we can find a lower bound for all products per⁡(AI,I)​per⁡(AI¯,I¯)\perm(A_{I,I})\perm(A_{\bar{I},\bar{I}}):

per⁡(AI,I)​per⁡(AI¯,I¯)≥per⁡(A[n]∩2​ℤ,[n]∩2​ℤ)​per⁡(A[n]∖2​ℤ,[n]∖2​ℤ).\perm(A_{I,I})\perm(A_{\bar{I},\bar{I}})\;\geq\;\perm(A_{[n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z},[n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z}})\perm(A_{[n]\smallsetminus 2\mathbb{Z},[n]\smallsetminus 2\mathbb{Z}}). (1.2)

Our main result in Section 5 shows that inequalities of the form (1.2) hold when

  1. (1)

    The totally nonnegative matrix AA is related to a unit interval order, and

  2. (2)

    II is the interval [h][h] for any h∈[n]h\in[n].

We conjecture the inequalities to hold for all totally nonnegative matrices and I=[h]I=[h]. On the other hand, we show that the inequalities do not hold for general II, even when restricted to matrices of the form (1).

2 Four families of sets counted by Catalan numbers

A simple subset of n×nn\times n totally nonnegative matrices is the set of 00-11 matrices which are weakly increasing in columns, weakly decreasing in rows, and all entries on or below the diagonal are 11. Call this set 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n}. For A∈𝒜nA\in\mathcal{A}_{n}, the boundary between entries of AA equal to 11 and 00 can be viewed as a 2​n2n-step Dyck path, consisting of nn horizontal and nn vertical steps, none below the diagonal, from the upper left corner of the matrix to the lower right corner. For example, we can draw an 88-step Dyck path on a matrix in 𝒜4\mathcal{A}_{4}.

The bijection between 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n} and 2​n2n-step Dyck paths implies that the cardinality of 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n} is the nnth Catalan number, 1n+1​(2​nn)\tfrac{1}{n+1}\tbinom{2n}{n}. (See [12, Exercise 6.19 (i)].)

Observation 2.1.

Each matrix in 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n} is totally nonnegative.

Elements of 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n} correspond bijectively to nn-element posets called unit interval orders. Call this set 𝒰n\mathcal{U}_{n}. (See [6, p. 33], [12, Exercise 6.19 (ddd)], [16, §8.2].) These are the posets in which no induced four-element subposet is isomorphic to either of the posets

The bijection A↦P⁡(A)A\mapsto P(A) is given by declaring i≤P⁡(A)ji\leq_{P(A)}j if and only if ai,j=0a_{i,j}=0. Each matrix AA is said to be the antiadjacency matrix of P⁡(A)P(A).

Define a planar network of order nn to be a directed, planar, acyclic multigraph which can be embedded in a disc so that 2​n2n boundary vertices can be labeled clockwise as source 1,…,1,\dotsc, source nn, sink n,…,n,\dotsc, sink 11. We will assume all sources to have indegree 00 and outdegree 11, and all sinks to have indegree 11 and outdegree 00. Let ℱn\mathcal{F}_{n} denote the set of such networks.

For each subinterval [a,b][a,b] of [n][n] we define a simple star network F[a,b]∈ℱnF_{[a,b]}\in\mathcal{F}_{n} by

  1. 1.

    Sources 1,…,n1,\dotsc,n lie on a vertical line to the left; sinks 1,…,n1,\dotsc,n lie on a vertical line to the right. Both are labeled from bottom to top.

  2. 2.

    An interior vertex lies between the sources and sinks.

  3. 3.

    For i=1,…,a−1i=1,\dotsc,a-1 and i=b+1,…,ni=b+1,\dotsc,n, a directed edge begins at source ii and terminates at sink ii.

  4. 4.

    For i=a,…,bi=a,\dotsc,b, a directed edge begins at source ii and terminates at the interior vertex, and another directed edge begins at the interior vertex and terminates at sink ii.

For zero- and one-element subintervals we define the trivial network F∅=F[1,1]=⋯=F[n,n]F_{\emptyset}=F_{[1,1]}=\cdots=F_{[n,n]} to have no interior vertex, and nn horizontal edges, each from source ii to sink ii, for i=1,…,ni=1,\dotsc,n. where F∅=F[1,1]=F[2,2]=F[3,3]=F[4,4]F_{\emptyset}=F_{[1,1]}=F_{[2,2]}=F_{[3,3]}=F_{[4,4]}. When there is no danger of confusion, we will omit source and sink labels as well.

The set ℱn\mathcal{F}_{n} is generated by simple star networks and two types of concatenation operations. Given networks E,F∈ℱnE,F\in\mathcal{F}_{n}, define the (ordinary) concatenation E∘FE\circ F as follows. For i=1,…,ni=1,\dotsc,n, do

  1. 1.

    Remove sink ii of EE and source ii of FF,

  2. 2.

    Merge each edge (x,sink ​i)(x,\text{sink }i) in EE with each edge (source ​i,y)(\text{source }i,y) in FF to form a single edge (x,y)(x,y) in E∘FE\circ F.

Sometimes in a concatenation E∘FE\circ F, there may exist vertices xx in EE, yy in FF with more than one edge incident upon both. Let m⁡(x,y)m(x,y) be this number. Define the condensed concatenation E∙FE\bullet F to be the subdigraph of E∘FE\circ F obtained by removing, for all such pairs (x,y)(x,y), all but one of the m⁡(x,y)m(x,y) edges incident upon both. For example, in ℱ4\mathcal{F}_{4} we have

(2.2)
Definition 2.2.

Define a descending star network to be a condensed concatenation of the form

F=F[c1,d1]∙⋯∙F[ct,dt],F=F_{[c_{1},d_{1}]}\bullet\cdots\bullet F_{[c_{t},d_{t}]},\\ (2.3)

with intervals [c1,d1],…,[ct,dt][c_{1},d_{1}],\dotsc,[c_{t},d_{t}] distinct, pairwise nonnesting, and satisfying c1>⋯>ctc_{1}>\cdots>c_{t}.

Let 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} be the set of all descending star networks of order nn. In the notation of Definition 2.2, these are F[1,4]F_{[1,4]}, F[2,4]∙F[1,3]F_{[2,4]}\bullet F_{[1,3]}, F[2,4]∙F[1,2]F_{[2,4]}\bullet F_{[1,2]}, etc. By [4, Thm. 3.6], [11, Thm. 3.5, Lem 5.3], the number of descending star networks of order nn is 1n+1​(2​nn)\tfrac{1}{n+1}\tbinom{2n}{n}. Explicit bijections between 𝒰n\mathcal{U}_{n} and 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} can be found at [3].

Given a planar network FF of order nn, define the path matrix B=(bi,j)B=(b_{i,j}) of FF by

bi,j=number of paths in F from source i to sink j.b_{i,j}=\text{number of paths in $F$ from source $i$ to sink $j$}. (2.4)

Let 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} be the set of 1n+1​(2​nn)\tfrac{1}{n+1}\tbinom{2n}{n} path matrices of planar networks in 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n}.

Some, but not all, of the matrices in 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n} appear in 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n}. The precise connection between 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n} and 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} can be described using block structures of these matrices. Let α=(α1,…,αr)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{r}) be an integer composition of nn, and define the (ordered) set partition (I1,…,Ir)(I_{1},\dotsc,I_{r}) of [n][n] into intervals of lengths α1,…,αr\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{r} by

I1=[1,α1],I2=[α1+1,α1+α2],…,Ir=[n−αr,n].I_{1}=[1,\alpha_{1}],\quad I_{2}=[\alpha_{1}+1,\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}],\quad\dotsc,\quad I_{r}=[n-\alpha_{r},n]. (2.5)

For any n×nn\times n matrix AA, we can write it in terms of block submatrices AIi,IjA_{I_{i},I_{j}} by

A=(AIi,Ij)=[AI1,I1AI1,I2⋯AI1,IrAI2,I1AI2,I2⋯AI1,IrAIr,I1AIr,I2⋯AIr,Ir].A=(A_{I_{i},I_{j}})=\begin{bmatrix}A_{I_{1},I_{1}}&A_{I_{1},I_{2}}&\cdots&A_{I_{1},I_{r}}\\ A_{I_{2},I_{1}}&A_{I_{2},I_{2}}&\cdots&A_{I_{1},I_{r}}\\ \vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\ A_{I_{r},I_{1}}&A_{I_{r},I_{2}}&\cdots&A_{I_{r},I_{r}}\end{bmatrix}. (2.6)

If AIi,Ij=0A_{I_{i},I_{j}}=0 whenever i<ji<j, we say AA is α\alpha-block lower-triangular; if AA and A⊤A^{\negthickspace\top\negthickspace} are both α\alpha-block lower-triangular, we say that AA is α\alpha-block diagonal. In particular, for any square matrix AA there is a finest composition α=α⁡(A)\alpha=\alpha(A) of nn for which AA is α\alpha-block lower-triangular. Next, we precisely state the relationship between 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n} and 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n}. Define the map

ψ:𝒜n\displaystyle\psi:\mathcal{A}_{n} →𝒫n\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathcal{P}_{n} (2.7)
A\displaystyle A ↦AI1,I1⊕⋯⊕AIr,Ir,\displaystyle\mapsto A_{I_{1},I_{1}}\oplus\cdots\oplus A_{I_{r},I_{r}},

where (I1,…,Ir)(I_{1},\dotsc,I_{r}) is the set partition associated to the finest composition α⁡(A)\alpha(A) as in (2.5).

Proposition 2.3.

Given unit interval order P∈𝒰nP\in\mathcal{U}_{n} with antiadjacency matrix AA, the descending star network F=F⁡(P)∈𝒟nF=F(P)\in\mathcal{D}_{n} has path matrix ψ⁡(A)\psi(A).

3 Permanents and path families

The planar networks defined in Section 2 have close connections to permanents. Let π=(π1,…,πn)\pi=(\pi_{1},\dotsc,\pi_{n}) be a sequence of source-to-sink paths in a planar network F∈ℱnF\in\mathcal{F}_{n}. We call π\pi a path family if there exists a permutation w=w1⋯wn∈𝔖nw=w_{1}\cdots w_{n}\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} such that πi\pi_{i} is a path from source ii to sink wiw_{i}. In this case, we say that π\pi has type ww. Further, we say that the path family covers FF if it contains every edge exactly once.

Let FF be a planar network of order nn and let I,JI,J be subsets of [n][n] with |I|=|J||I|=|J|. Let ΠI,J​(F)\Pi_{I,J}(F) denote the set of path families from sources indexed by II to sinks indexed by JJ. The following interpretation of the determinent is due to Karlin and McGregor [7] and usually attributed to Lindstrom [8].

Lemma 3.1.

For I,J⊆[n]I,J\subseteq[n] with |I|=|J|=k|I|=|J|=k, we have

det(AI,J)=#{π=(π1,…,πk)∈ΠI,J(F)|π1,…,πk pairwise nonintersecting }.\det(A_{I,J})=\#\{\pi=(\pi_{1},\dotsc,\pi_{k})\in\Pi_{I,J}(F)\,|\,\pi_{1},\dotsc,\pi_{k}\text{ pairwise nonintersecting }\}.

We have the following combinatorial interpretation of the permanent using path families.

Lemma 3.2.

For I,J⊆[n]I,J\subseteq[n] with |I|=|J|=k|I|=|J|=k, we have per⁡(AI,J)=|ΠI,J​(F)|\perm(A_{I,J})=|\Pi_{I,J}(F)|.

There is a simple formula counting path families covering a descending star network.

Lemma 3.3.

Given descending star network F=F[c1,d1]∙⋯∙F[cr,dr]F=F_{[c_{1},d_{1}]}\bullet\cdots\bullet F_{[c_{r},d_{r}]}, define m1,…,mr,k1,…,kr−1m_{1},\dotsc,m_{r},k_{1},\dotsc,k_{r-1} by

mi=di−ci+1,ki=max⁡{di+1−ci+1,0}.m_{i}=d_{i}-c_{i}+1,\quad k_{i}=\max\{d_{i+1}-c_{i}+1,0\}. (3.1)

Then we have

|Π[n],[n]​(F)|=m1!⋯mr−1!k1!⋯kr−1!⋅mr!.|\Pi_{[n],[n]}(F)|=\frac{m_{1}!\cdots m_{r-1}!}{k_{1}!\cdots k_{r-1}!}\cdot m_{r}!. (3.2)

Let h∈[n]h\in[n], then define sets J=[h]J=[h], J¯=[h+1,n]\bar{J}=[h+1,n], I=[n]∩2​ℤI=[n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z}, and I¯=[n]∖2​ℤ\bar{I}=[n]\smallsetminus 2\mathbb{Z}. Lemma 3.3 and several factorial inequalities yield the following relation for path families.

Lemma 3.4.

Fix h∈[n]h\in[n] and let F=F[c1,d1]∙⋯∙F[cr,dr]F=F_{[c_{1},d_{1}]}\bullet\cdots\bullet F_{[c_{r},d_{r}]} be a descending star network such that F[cp,dp]F_{[c_{p},d_{p}]} is the only star with [cp,dp]∩[h,h+1]≠∅[c_{p},d_{p}]\cap[h,h+1]\neq\emptyset. We have

|ΠI,I​(F)|⋅|ΠI¯,I¯​(F)|≤|ΠJ,J​(F)|⋅|ΠJ¯,J¯​(F)|.|\Pi_{I,I}(F)|\cdot|\Pi_{\bar{I},\bar{I}}(F)|\leq|\Pi_{J,J}(F)|\cdot|\Pi_{\bar{J},\bar{J}}(F)|.

4 Merging stars in a star network

For a general descending star network FF, there may be multiple stars F[cp,dp]F_{[c_{p},d_{p}]} with [cp,dp]∩[h,h+1]≠∅[c_{p},d_{p}]\cap[h,h+1]\neq\emptyset. We now define a function that can modify the star network FF. For each number h∈[n]h\in[n], define the hh-merge function ϕh:𝒟n→𝒟n\phi_{h}:\mathcal{D}_{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{n} as follows.

  1. 1.

    Given F=F[c1,d1]∙⋯∙F[cr,dr]F=F_{[c_{1},d_{1}]}\bullet\cdots\bullet F_{[c_{r},d_{r}]}, define

    p\displaystyle p =max⁡{k|[ck,dk]∩[h,h+1]≠∅},\displaystyle=\max\{k\,|\,[c_{k},d_{k}]\cap[h,h+1]\neq\emptyset\}, q\displaystyle q =min⁡{k|[ck,dk]∩[h,h+1]≠∅}.\displaystyle=\min\{k\,|\,[c_{k},d_{k}]\cap[h,h+1]\neq\emptyset\}.
  2. 2.

    Define ϕh(F)=F[c1,d1]∙⋯∙F[cq−1,dq−1]∙F[cp,dq]∙F[cp+1,dp+1]∙⋯∙F[cr,dr]\phi_{h}(F)=F_{[c_{1},d_{1}]}\bullet\cdots\bullet F_{[c_{q-1},d_{q-1}]}\bullet F_{[c_{p},d_{q}]}\bullet F_{[c_{p+1},d_{p+1}]}\bullet\cdots\bullet F_{[c_{r},d_{r}]}.

The hh-merge function gives an equality on the cardinality of path families

Proposition 4.1.

Fix h∈[n]h\in[n], and let FF be a descending star network of order nn with path matrix AA. Let BB be the path matrix of the descending star network ϕh​(F)\phi_{h}(F). Then we have

  1. (i)

    A[h],[h]=B[h],[h]A_{[h],[h]}=B_{[h],[h]} and A[h+1,n],[h+1,n]=B[h+1,n],[h+1,n]A_{[h+1,n],[h+1,n]}=B_{[h+1,n],[h+1,n]}.

  2. (ii)

    |Π[h],[h]​(F)|⋅|Π[h+1,n],[h+1,n]​(F)|=|Π[h],[h]​(ϕh​(F))|⋅|Π[h+1,n],[h+1,n]​(ϕh​(F))||\Pi_{[h],[h]}(F)|\cdot|\Pi_{[h+1,n],[h+1,n]}(F)|=|\Pi_{[h],[h]}(\phi_{h}(F))|\cdot|\Pi_{[h+1,n],[h+1,n]}(\phi_{h}(F))|.

5 Main results

Now we state our main result about products of permanents.

Theorem 5.1.

Let AA be the antiadjacency matrix of a unit interval order. Fix h∈[n]h\in[n] and define sets

J=[h],I=[n]∩2​ℤ.J=[h],\qquad I=[n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z}.

Then we have

per⁡(AJ,J)​per⁡(AJ¯,J¯)≥per⁡(AI,I)​per⁡(AI¯,I¯).\perm(A_{J,J})\perm(A_{\bar{J},\bar{J}})\geq\perm(A_{I,I})\perm(A_{\bar{I},\bar{I}}). (5.1)

Proof omitted.

Theorem 5.2.

Let AA be the antiadjacency matrix of a unit interval order. Let I=[n]∩2​ℤI=[n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z}. Then for any i∈[n]i\in[n], we have

per⁡(A[n]∖{i},[n]∖{i})​per⁡(A{i},{i})≥per⁡(AI,I)​per⁡(AI¯,I¯).\perm(A_{[n]\setminus\{i\},[n]\setminus\{i\}})\perm(A_{\{i\},\{i\}})\geq\perm(A_{I,I})\perm(A_{\bar{I},\bar{I}}). (5.2)

Proof omitted.

6 A Generalization on II

A natural generalization of a product of two permanents indexed by even or odd integers is a product of ss permanents indexed by integers which are equivalent modulo ss. Define

[c,d]rs={x∈[c,d]:x≡r⁡(mod ​s)}.[c,d]_{r}^{s}=\{x\in[c,d]:\ x\equiv r\ (\text{mod }s)\}.

Next, we have a generalization of Lemma 3.3.

Lemma 6.1.

Let F=F[c0,d0]∙⋯∙F[ct,dt]F=F_{[c_{0},d_{0}]}\bullet\cdots\bullet F_{[c_{t},d_{t}]} be a descending star network. Fix s∈[n]s\in[n]. For every r∈[0,s−1]r\in[0,s-1], We have

|Π[1,n]rs,[1,n]rs​(F)|=|[c0,d0]rs|!⋅|[c1,d1]rs|!⋯|[ct,dt]rs|!|[c0,d1]rs|!⋅|[c1,d2]rs|!⋯|[ct−1,dt]rs|!.|\Pi_{[1,n]_{r}^{s},[1,n]_{r}^{s}}(F)|=\frac{|[c_{0},d_{0}]_{r}^{s}|!\cdot|[c_{1},d_{1}]_{r}^{s}|!\cdots|[c_{t},d_{t}]_{r}^{s}|!}{|[c_{0},d_{1}]_{r}^{s}|!\cdot|[c_{1},d_{2}]_{r}^{s}|!\cdots|[c_{t-1},d_{t}]_{r}^{s}|!}. (6.1)

We can now extend Theorem 5.1 to a more general result.

Theorem 6.2.

Let AA be the antiadjacency matrix of an nn-element unit interval order.

Then for s=2,…,n−1s=2,\ldots,n-1, we have

per(A[1,n]0s,[1,n]0s)⋯per(A[1,n]s−1s,[1,n]s−1s)≥per(A[1,n]0s+1,[1,n]0s+1)⋯per(A[1,n]ss+1,[1,n]ss+1).\perm(A_{[1,n]_{0}^{s},[1,n]_{0}^{s}})\cdots\perm(A_{[1,n]_{s-1}^{s},[1,n]_{s-1}^{s}})\geq\perm(A_{[1,n]_{0}^{s+1},[1,n]_{0}^{s+1}})\cdots\perm(A_{[1,n]_{s}^{s+1},[1,n]_{s}^{s+1}}). (6.2)

Proof omitted.

7 A Generalization to all TNN matrices

In this section, we will show that (1.2) holds for I=[1,⌊n2⌋]I=[1,\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor].

A polynomial p⁡(x11,x12,⋯,xn​n)p(x_{11},x_{12},\cdots,x_{nn}) in n2n^{2} variables is called totally non-negative (TNN) if it satisfies

p⁡(A):=p⁡(a11,a12,⋯,an​n)≥0p(A):=p(a_{11},a_{12},\cdots,a_{nn})\geq 0 (7.1)

for each n×nn\times n totally non-negative matrix A=(ai​j)A=(a_{ij}). Therefore, (1.2) is true if and only if the polynomial

per⁡(X[1,⌊n2⌋],[1,⌊n2⌋])​per⁡(X[⌈n2⌉,n],[⌈n2⌉,n])−per⁡(X[n]∩2​ℤ,[n]∩2​ℤ)​per⁡(X[n]∖2​ℤ,[n]∖2​ℤ)\perm(X_{[1,\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor],[1,\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor]})\perm(X_{[\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil,n],[\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil,n]})-\perm(X_{[n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z},[n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z}})\perm(X_{[n]\setminus 2\mathbb{Z},[n]\setminus 2\mathbb{Z}}) (7.2)

is TNN.

Drake, Gerrish and Skandera [5] gave a necessary and sufficient condition for a polynomial which is a difference of “permutation monomials” to be TNN.

Theorem 7.1 (Drake, Gerrish, Skandera).

Let ww and uu be two permutations in 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}. Then ww is less than or equal to uu in the Bruhat order if and only if the polynomial

x1,w1⋯xn,wn−x1,u1⋯xn,unx_{1,w_{1}}\cdots x_{n,w_{n}}-x_{1,u_{1}}\cdots x_{n,u_{n}}

is totally non-negative.

Let t=⌊n2⌋t=\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\rfloor. The term per⁡(X⌊n2⌋,⌊n2⌋)​per⁡(X⌈n2⌉,⌈n2⌉)\perm(X_{\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor,\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor})\perm(X_{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil,\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil}) contains monomials x1,w1⋯xt,wtxt+1,wt+1⋯xn,wnx_{1,w_{1}}\cdots x_{t,w_{t}}x_{t+1,w_{t+1}}\cdots x_{n,w_{n}} such that

w1⋯wtpermutes{1,…,t},wt+1⋯wnpermutes{t+1,…,n}.w_{1}\cdots w_{t}\ \ \text{permutes}\ \{1,\dotsc,t\},\qquad w_{t+1}\cdots w_{n}\ \ \text{permutes}\ \{t+1,\dotsc,n\}.

For convenience, we set

𝔄n=𝔖1,…,t×𝔖t+1,…,n={w∈𝔖n|w1⋯wtpermutes{1,…,t}andwt+1⋯wnpermutes{t+1,…,n}}.\begin{split}&\mathfrak{A}_{n}=\mathfrak{S}_{1,\dotsc,t}\times\mathfrak{S}_{t+1,\dotsc,n}\\ =\{&w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\ |\ w_{1}\cdots w_{t}\ \text{permutes}\ \{1,\dotsc,t\}\ \text{and}\ w_{t+1}\cdots w_{n}\ \text{permutes}\ \{t+1,\dotsc,n\}\}.\end{split} (7.3)

Also, for future reference, we define

𝔄~n={w∈𝔖n|w1⋯wt+1permutes{1,…,t+1}andwt+2⋯wnpermutes{t+2,…,n}}.\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}_{n}=\{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\ |\ w_{1}\cdots w_{t+1}\ \text{permutes}\ \{1,\dotsc,t+1\}\ \text{and}\ w_{t+2}\cdots w_{n}\ \text{permutes}\ \{t+2,\dotsc,n\}\}. (7.4)

It is easy to see that |𝔄n|=⌊n2⌋!​⌈n2⌉!|\mathfrak{A}_{n}|=\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\rfloor!\lceil\tfrac{n}{2}\rceil!. For example, 𝔄4={1234,1243,2134,2143}\mathfrak{A}_{4}=\{1234,1243,2134,2143\}. The product of permanents per⁡(X[n]∩2​ℤ,[n]∩2​ℤ)​per⁡(X[n]∖2​ℤ,[n]∖2​ℤ)\perm(X_{[n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z},[n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z}})\perm(X_{[n]\setminus 2\mathbb{Z},[n]\setminus 2\mathbb{Z}}) contains monomials x1,u1⋯xn,unx_{1,u_{1}}\cdots x_{n,u_{n}} such that

u1u3u5⋯permutes{1,3,5,⋯}=[n]∖2ℤ,u2u4u6⋯permutes{2,4,6,⋯}=[n]∩2ℤ.u_{1}u_{3}u_{5}\cdots\ \text{permutes}\ \{1,3,5,\cdots\}=[n]\setminus 2\mathbb{Z},\quad u_{2}u_{4}u_{6}\cdots\ \text{permutes}\ \{2,4,6,\cdots\}=[n]\cap 2\mathbb{Z}.

We call the set that consists of u=u1⋯unu=u_{1}\cdots u_{n} satisfying the above conditions 𝔅n\mathfrak{B}_{n}, i,e,

𝔅n={u∈𝔖n|u1u2⋯untakes odd and even integers alternately and u1 is odd}\mathfrak{B}_{n}=\{u\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\ |\ u_{1}u_{2}\cdots u_{n}\ \text{takes odd and even integers alternately and $u_{1}$ is odd}\} (7.5)

It is easy to see that |𝔅n|=⌊n2⌋!​⌈n2⌉!|\mathfrak{B}_{n}|=\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\rfloor!\lceil\tfrac{n}{2}\rceil!. Then, the polynomial (7.2) has this number of positive terms (on the left) and negative terms (on the right). Therefore, if we can find a bijective map fn:𝔄n→𝔅nf_{n}:\mathfrak{A}_{n}\rightarrow\mathfrak{B}_{n}, such that w≤fn​(w)w\leq f_{n}(w) for all w∈𝔄nw\in\mathfrak{A}_{n}, by Theorem 7.1, the polynomial (7.2) is TNN.

Next, we introduce a few necessary maps. For p,q∈[n]p,q\in[n], define an insertion map insp\mathrm{ins}_{p} and an insertion-swapping map inssq\mathrm{inss}_{q} (when n+1−qn+1-q is even) given by

insp:𝔖n\displaystyle\mathrm{ins}_{p}:\mathfrak{S}_{n} →𝔖n+1,\displaystyle\to\mathfrak{S}_{n+1},
w=w1⋯wp⋯wn\displaystyle w=w_{1}\cdots w_{p}\cdots w_{n} ↦w1⋯wp−1(n+1)wp⋯wn,\displaystyle\mapsto w_{1}\cdots w_{p-1}(n+1)w_{p}\cdots w_{n},
inssq:𝔖n\displaystyle\text{inss}_{q}:\mathfrak{S}_{n} →𝔖n+1,\displaystyle\to\mathfrak{S}_{n+1},

Our algorithm behaves nicely with respect to inversion and the Bruhat order. We have the following partial results and conjecture for the function fnf_{n} defined by Algorithm 7.5.

Theorem 7.6.

For all w∈𝔄n∖{e}w\in\mathfrak{A}_{n}\setminus\{e\}, we have inv​(w)<inv​(fn​(w))\textsc{inv}(w)<\textsc{inv}(f_{n}(w)).

Proof omitted.

Theorem 7.7.

For n≤13n\leq 13 and all w∈𝔄nw\in\mathfrak{A}_{n}, we have w≤fn​(w)w\leq f_{n}(w) in the Bruhat order.

Proof omitted.

Conjecture 7.8.

For all nn and all w∈𝔄nw\in\mathfrak{A}_{n} we have w≤fn​(w)w\leq f_{n}(w) in the Bruhat order.

A proof of Conjecture 7.8 would extend Theorem 5.1 to all totally nonnegative matrices.
